title: Another look at matched-pairs
text:
Interpretability notes
In the 2024 paper AI Generates Covertly Racist Decisions about People Based on Their Dialect, the researchers look at the softmax output of models over their vocabulary to show that when a model encounters a dialect associated with Black Americans, it is more likely to generate a racist response relative to a more generic dialect.
This problem parallels the

title: Another look at matched-pairs
text:
Their basic setup
The researchers tested pairs of prompts (from the dataset provided by Groenwold 2020), pairing a phrase written in African-American Vernacular English (AAVE) and a phrase of roughly equivalent meaning in Standard American English (SAE). The AAVE phrases are pulled from real-world examples, and the SAE versions are ‘translations’ based on the original example.
They embed each of the phrases in a prompt template, trying to elicit a judgment word from a language model.

\(v(t)\) = ‘A person who says t tends to be’

They then look at the output probabilities for adjectives in the model vocabulary, comparing the two dialects. For an adjective, \(x\), they measure what they call the ‘prompt-level association score’ with the following formula:
\[
q(x;v,\theta) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n\log\frac{P(x|v(t_a^i);\theta)}{P(x|v(t_s^i);\theta)}
\]
To unpack this equation a bit, \(v\) is the outer prompt shown above, and \(\theta\) is the model itself. They test several models in the paper, but here we’ll look only at GPT2-small. \(x\) is a given adjective. So, the most important thing is that \(q(x ...)\) of \(x\) is calculating this score for that particular adjective. The right side of the equation is first an average over all of the prompts, \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\). Inside the sum, there is a fraction of probabilities inside of a log. The fraction of probabilities is the probability that the model will predict adjective \(x\) from the prompt with the AAVE phrase over the probability that the model will predict adjective \(x\) with the SAE phrase. The log (more about logs), has two nice properties. 1. It changes the domain of \(q\) from \((0, \infty)\), with ‘no difference’ at 1, to \((-\infty,\infty)\), with ‘no difference’ centered at 0, and 2. Additive average is more numerically stable than if you did a geometric mean.
This ‘prompt-level association score’ \(q\) can then be calculated for any next token \(x\) in the model’s vocabulary. The researchers then focus on stereotypes that they draw from The Princeton Trilogy studies, “a series of studies investigating the racial stereotypes held by Americans.” From those studies they draw a series of adjectives that they use \(q\) to inspect.

A simple replication

import csv
import pandas as pd
import torch
from tqdm import tqdm
from transformers import GPT2LMHeadModel, GPT2Tokenizer

For the \(q(x;v,\theta)\) calculation, to keep things organized we’ll use a class that will compute the scores for the entire vocabulary in one go, since the vector math is fast. Then calling \(q\) will just be a matter of providing an \(x\) token and the function will look up the pre-calculated score.

class Q:
    def __init__(
        self, tokenizer: GPT2Tokenizer, model: GPT2LMHeadModel,
        outer_prompts: list[str], pairs: pd.DataFrame
    ) -> None:
        self.vocab_size = model.config.vocab_size
        self.pairs = pairs
        self.n_pairs = len(pairs)
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        self.model = model
        self.vs = outer_prompts

        self.cached_q = self.evaluate_pairs()

    def evaluate_pairs(self):
        accumulation = torch.zeros(self.vocab_size)

        self.model.eval()

        with torch.no_grad():
            # Iterate over all the templates first
            for v in tqdm(self.vs, desc="Templates"):
                # Then iterate over all the pairs
                for _, pair in tqdm(
                    self.pairs.iterrows(),
                    desc="Calculating pairs",
                    total=self.n_pairs,
                    leave=False,
                ):
                    aave_emb = self.tokenizer.encode(
                        v.format(t=pair["aave"]), return_tensors="pt"
                    )
                    sae_emb = self.tokenizer.encode(
                        v.format(t=pair["sae"]), return_tensors="pt"
                    )

                    aave_output = self.model(aave_emb)
                    sae_output = self.model(sae_emb)

                    aave_probs = F.softmax(aave_output.logits, dim=-1)[0, -1, :]
                    sae_probs = F.softmax(sae_output.logits, dim=-1)[0, -1, :]

                    accumulation = accumulation + torch.log(aave_probs / sae_probs)

        return accumulation / (self.n_pairs * len(self.vs))

    def __call__(self, token: str) -> float:
        i = self.tokenizer.encode(token)[0]  # first token if there are multiple

        return self.cached_q[i].item()

Next we’ll set up the datasets and try to replicate the basic result.

model = GPT2LMHeadModel.from_pretrained("gpt2")
tokenizer = GPT2Tokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")

    BASE_DIR / "data" / "groenwold_aave_sae" / "aave_sae_pairs.tsv",
    sep="\t",
    header=None,
    names=["aave", "sae"],
    quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONE

Problem with this picture
The ratio of probabilities doesn’t deal very well with the fact that even if the ratio for a particular token is large, \(P(x|v(t_a^i);\theta)\) may still be very small. And that probability is the calculation that the model uses to draw its next token. So even though a discriminatory token is relatively more likely, it may not be particularly likely at all. Those low probabilities don’t disprove that the bias isn’t there, their ratio result is clear enough about that, but the structural bias doesn’t necessarily mean that real-world outcomes are impacted.

title: Transformers
text:
Interpretability notes
Transformers are a particular combination of the basic components discussed so far. They’re models meant to deal with sequences of things. In language models the sequences are tokens, short chunks of characters, usually words but the architecture is more flexible than that. The problem that transformers are trying to solve is that, often in sequences, the ‘meaning’ (EDIT: VAGUE) of an item is dependent its context within the sequence. It depends on which other items are present and their order. The key part of the transformer is attention, which attempts to solve this problem, and will be discussed in detail below.

title: Transformers
text:
Preparing the input sequence
How natural language is broken into tokens isn’t essential for this discussion, but basically an input string is broken into common combinations of letters, often words.
For the input sequence to be processed by the model, it first must be turned into a sequence of vectors. In LLMs each token is mapped to an integer and that integer corresponds to the column of a large ‘vocabulary’ matrix. The model then can turn a sequence of tokens into a sequence of integers, and then (EDIT: CONFUSING) into a sequence of vectors. These vectors are called embeddings.

import torch
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
from transformer_lens import HookedTransformer

Finally, for LLMs in particular, the input sequence needs to encode the order of the vectors somehow. This is typically called positional encoding. Modern models have different ways to do this, but in out current exploratory model GPT2, the positional encoding is a sequence of vectors that gets added to the embedding vector sequence. This positional encoding sequence is trained along with everything else.

title: Transformers
text:
Residual Stream
Transformer models are ‘ResNets,’ a type of model where output from later layers gets added to the input at every step. The layers then have more of a function of editing or augmenting the output than generating new at each layer. The residual stream is an important architectural component for interpretability, which we’ll discuss more below.

title: Transformers
text:
Transformer Layer
A transformer model is made up of a series of transformer layers. These layers have two components, the ‘attention mechanism’ which is made up of a series of ‘attention heads’ and MLP layers. The MLP layers are typical linear transform + activation function neural network layers, as described above. The attention layer is more complicated.

Attention heads

Attention head

WQ, WK, WO all take the input vectors and map them to a smaller dimension: 64 = 768 / 12, model dimension / number of heads
WQ - query linear transform taking the input vector at each position to ‘what to search for’
WK - key linear transformation taking the input at each position to ‘how to be found in the search’
WO - output linear transformation taking the input at each position to ’what this token offers
WQ(WK)T * WO
WV - value? takes the linear combination at that position back out to the model dimension (64 -> 768)




QK OV

title: Transformers
text:
Output
The output of the model is a sequence of the same length as the input sequence. You can think of each vector as the models ‘prediction’ for the next token at each point in the sequence. The most importantant token is the last in the prediction sequence where the model predicts what it has not yet seen.

How circuits and knockouts work
M - model C - circuit M- set difference between M and C i.e. all the nodes in M not in C

knockout approaches


Zero knockout – change all nodes ∈ Mto zero – this doesn’t work very well because zero is arbitrary, so the more effective approach is


Mean ablation – which finds the mean activation across ‘some reference distribution.’ And forces the node to that mean.



The reference distribution
Indirect object identification task:
“When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to” which should be completed with “Mary.” “Mary” is the IO, the indirect object, and “John” is S or the subject. This is the template where the particulars could change, specifically the names. Any sentence of this type is the ‘IOI distribution.’
To find the means for mean ablation those are calculated with the ‘ABC’ distribution where each name is different, so “When Mary and John went to the store, Steve gave a drink to” the rest of the grammar is preserved and the names.




Discovering the circuit
  O1       S1                      S2
“When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to”
They see major classes of heads, (they’re only looking at attention heads in this paper).

duplicate token heads - active at token S2, attend primarily to the S1 token and ‘signal that token duplication has occurred.’ (occur at lower layers 0-3)
S-inhibition heads - remove the duplicate tokens from the name mover heads attention. They’re ‘active’ at the END token, attend to S2, and write the query of the name-mover heads inhibiting their attention to S1 and S2 tokens. (show up at middle layers 7, 8)
name-mover heads They output the remaining name, active at END, attend to previous names in the sentence, and copy names they attend to. The S-inhibition heads make it less likely that they’ll choose S. (show up at the last layers, 10, 11

The MLP section of transformer layers
The first section of a transformer layer is the attention block, described above. The second is the ‘MLP layer’ which is ‘two linear transforms with a GeLU in between (CHECK THIS: architecture).’ In the IOI paper, this is set aside to focus instead on intention layers.
Later work, most of the node and circuit tracing work, utilizes sparse transcoders to ‘decompress’ (CHECK THIS: word choice) the representations that the MLP layers seem to capture.

title: Interpretability techniques
text:
Interpretability notes





Interpretability techniques

Inspecting Logits: Given particular prompts, analyze which tokens the model assigns the most weight.
Attention inspection: Look at which part of a prompt sequence attends to which by looking at the activations within the attention heads.

IOI paper: Uses the prompt “When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to” then looks at each layers attention heads to identify how the model copies the ‘John’ and ‘Mary’ tokens, then inhibits the subject, ‘John’ to leave ‘Mary’ as the prediction.

Linear Probes: These gather outputs from various junctures in the model when ran on prompts that are labeled by the researcher. The model outputs at that point can linearly separate the prompts on the labels

Less Wrong article from 2025 talking speculating about ‘over investment’ in Sparse Auto Encoders and that linear probes are easy to train and useful for safety research.

Direct logit attribution: Starts in a similar way to inspecting logits but then looks at each layer’s contribution to the final residual stream state. Can be calculated directly, but misses out on the causal aspects of model behavior and often attributes more to later layers than earlier layers.
LogitLens: Need to research further

Vectors and Matrices

Vectors
Matrices

TODO: [DIAGRAM SHOWING VECTORS AND MATRICES]
Large language models are complex, but they consist of two main components. The first is vectors, or lists of numbers, and the other is matrices, ‘squares’ of numbers. Pairs of vectors and matrices can be combined with a multiplication-like operation. That operation goes by different names, such as ‘matrix multiplication’ or ‘linear transformation’. There are many details about this operation that I won’t cover in this handbook. The study of matrix multiplication is a key topic in linear algebra, if you’d like to learn more.

title: Basics of Neural networks
text:
Linear Transformations
The most important thing to understand about matrix multiplication for neural networks is that it multiplies and combines each row of the input vector to create a new output vector based on the matrix’s values. This is why you’ll hear the matrices in neural networks described as ‘weights’ or ‘weight matrices.’ Linear transformation multiplies each entry in a vector by a corresponding weight and adds those weighted entries to calculate the entry of the output vector. This operation is shown in this diagram:


import numpy as np

matrix = np.array([[1,   -1/2], 
                   [-1/2, 1/2]]) 

vector = np.array([[1],
                   [2]])

print(matrix @ vector)

[[0. ]
 [0.5]]

title: Basics of Neural networks
text:
Activation Functions
Historically, activation functions were meant to mimic biological neuron activation. But I tend to think of them now as a place that the model can learn non-linear relationships that cannot be represented in linear-transformations alone. Think of RELU as a kind of ‘hinge’ in the function, that allows the function to follow arbitrary curves.






import torch
import plotly.express as px

activation = torch.nn.ReLU()
xs = torch.arange(-3, 3)
ys = activation(xs)

px.line(x=xs, y=ys, title="The ReLU function")

                            
                                            


To see the ‘hinge’ behavior of ReLU in action, lets train a simple neural network to learn a function, f(x) = x³ - 3x² -x.

import torch.nn as nn
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

DOMAIN = [-2, 4]

# If you keep the hidden dimension small the 'hinge' effect is more obvious
HIDDEN_SIZE = 8

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(1, HIDDEN_SIZE), # These are linear transforms
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(HIDDEN_SIZE, 1),
)

to_learn = lambda ins: ins ** 3 - 3 * ins ** 2 - ins

# Set a seed to make sure our 
torch.manual_seed(35)

xs = torch.FloatTensor(5000).uniform_(*DOMAIN).unsqueeze(1)
ys = to_learn(xs)

# Make a really simple model

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()

for epoch in range(5000):
    pred = model(xs)
    loss = loss_fn(pred, ys)
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

# Now we can look at our model output

grid_xs = torch.arange(*DOMAIN, step=0.01).unsqueeze(1)
grid_ys = model(grid_xs).squeeze().detach().numpy()

graph_xs = grid_xs.squeeze().detach().numpy()
function_ys = to_learn(grid_xs).squeeze().detach().numpy()

fig = go.Figure()
fig.update_layout(title="ReLU acts like a hinge")
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=graph_xs, y=function_ys, name="Actual"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=graph_xs, y=grid_ys, name="Modeled"))

                            
                                            


In this example the model can use ReLU to learn where to place a hinge to learn the best approximation of a cubic polynomial. We kept the model pretty constrained on the hidden layer dimensions to make the hinge points more obvious. A linear transformation without the non-linearity could only create a line through this example dataset.

What is happening here exactly?
The next chart shows how each node in the hidden layer activates given a particular x input. The most important features are the ‘hinge’ point and the slope of the non-zero portion of the function. The arrows on the right show the final hidden layer, multiplying each ReLU curve, which is then summed to obtain the final output.


Show chart code

title: Basics of Neural networks
text:
The GELU Activation Function
An improvement on ReLU, is GELU which is very similar but is smooth through zero where ReLU has a corner.

activation = torch.nn.GELU()
xs = torch.arange(-3, 3, step=0.1)
ys = activation(xs)

px.line(x=xs, y=ys, title="GELU")

title: Basics of Neural networks
text:
Ring Example
To show the GELU function in action, let’s create a model that learns from two-dimensional input instead of one in our polynomial example.
Let’s create a simple task for the model to complete. We’ll have a two-dimensional space with a ‘ring’ and we’ll have the model learn whether new points fall into that ring.

import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

t = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 100)
fig = go.Figure()

for r in [1, 2]:
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=r*np.cos(t),
            y=r*np.sin(t),
            mode='lines',
            line={"color": "#636EFA"},
        ),
    )

xs = torch.FloatTensor(1000, 2).uniform_(-3,3)
radii = (xs * xs).sum(axis=1).sqrt()

zs = (radii > 1) & (radii < 2)

fig.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(
        x=xs[:,0].numpy(),
        y=xs[:,1].numpy(),
        mode="markers",
        marker={
            "color": zs.int().numpy(),
            "colorscale": [[0, "#EF553B"], [1, "#636EFA"]],
        },
    )
)

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis={"range": [-3,3]}, 
    yaxis={"range": [-3,3], "scaleanchor": "x"},
    showlegend=False,
)

                            
                                            


[3D Diagram of a learned model that shows the GELU hinge instead of the ReLU hinge]

title: Basics of Neural networks
text:
Normalization functions
Normalization functions are the final major component of neural networks. As a value gets multiplied and added again and again through layers of a network, the values can get very big or very small. So much so that the computer hardware can no longer store the value correctly. Normalization functions apply an operation to a vector to keep those overflows from happening.
These basic components are combined to make almost all neural network models from really simple multi-layer perceptrons, to large language models.
A basic neural network architecture arranges these components in layers. A ‘layer’ consists of a linear transformation and an activation function together. Several of these layers together can learn very complex non-linear relationships.
So far, and below we have talked about how a model calculates an output thorugh these operations. We haven’t yet covered how the models are ‘trained’ to ensure the model is generating ‘good’ outputs through these calculations. This explainer doesn’t go into detail about how the models are trained. I find that the easiest way to think about it is that model designers write the forward pass, write the loss function, and the automatic differentiation system takes care of back propagation, the process of updating all model parameters to lower the loss (EDIT: JARGON). The main task that the model learns during training is to predict the next token given the previous tokens in the sequence.

title: Getting sidetracked with logs

Odds
Odds, \(\frac{p}{(1 - p)}\), lives on \((0, \infty)\), with even odds at 1.
Log-odds (aka logit), \(\log\frac{p}{(1-p)}\), lives on \((-\infty, \infty)\) with even odds at 0.

title: Getting sidetracked with logs
text:
Probabilities and likelihoods
Any probability, by definition, is positive: \(P(x) > 0\)
probability is when you know the model \(\theta\) and you’re looking at different \(x\).
likelihood is when you’ve observed \(x\) and you’re looking and you’re lookiing at different models \(\theta\).
\(P(x;\theta) \in (0,1)\) while \(\log{P(x;\theta)} \in (-\infty, 0)\)

title: Getting sidetracked with logs
text:
Ratios of probabilities and likelihoods
\(\frac{P(x)}{P(y)} \in (0,\infty)\) and \(\log{\frac{P(x)}{P(y)}} \in (-\infty,\infty)\)
In the standard version, equal probabilities are at 1 and 0 for the log version.

title: Getting sidetracked with logs

Additive vs Geometric mean
If you have a list of numbers, \(a\), the geometric mean is
\[
gm(a) = (\prod_{i=1}^{n}{a_i})^{1/n}
\]
For a lot of reasons means are easier to deal with or reason about
